source.title: Probe before You Talk: Towards Black-box Defense against Backdoor Unalignment for Large Language Models
source.authors: Biao Yi; Tian-Sheng Huang; Si-Shuo Chen; Tong Li; Zhe-Li Liu; Zhixuan Chu; Yiming Li

record.tranche_reason: Tests a related safety-degradation behavior using trigger-conditioned backdoor fine-tuning and probe concatenation, rather than the original fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The study reports qualitative harmful compliance/refusal outcomes for trigger-conditioned backdoor models and first-output-token distribution distortions for the probe-concatenation effect. Its BEAT detector AUROC/TPR results measure detection performance, not harmful-compliance rates, so they are not rows for the claim versions. The jailbreak section reports detector performance on selected successfully attacked samples, not attack success or refusal rates. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: This is a backdoor-defense paper. It deliberately builds trigger-conditioned unalignment by SFT on 50 triggered harmful pairs, 50 safe refusals and 50 helpful samples, or uses RLHF-trojan models. Its outcomes are the BEAT detector's AUROC/TPR. The trigger-conditioned compliance is induced on purpose and is a different construct from V1's unconditional loss of refusal. No benign fine-tuning, aligned-vs-base per-position KL, prefill/decoding attack rates, parameter localization, cause of shallowness or deepening training is measured. The idea that aligned models refuse within the first few tokens is used as a design premise, not tested against a base model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that triggered samples sharply cut the backdoored model's refusal of a harmful probe (the probe concatenate effect). BEAT exploits this for black-box detection, averaging about 99.6% AUROC across SFT and RLHF backdoors. It also detects transfer jailbreaks, with AUROC 91-99%. It resists most adaptive attacks but fails when the attacker knows the probe (AUROC 42.6) and, at 10-token sampling, against a trained refusal prefix.
record.recipe_differences: Uses trigger-poisoned SFT or RLHF backdoor models and a black-box probe-concatenation detector; it does not reproduce harmful fine-tuning safety-loss measurements, aligned-versus-base position-wise KL, or safety-deepening training.
record.method_sensitivity: Probe choice and consistency, number of probes, number and length of sampled outputs, distance metric, temperature, and adaptive trigger/training strategies affect detector performance. The text reports that performance declines when sample length exceeds 10 in one ablation, and higher temperatures above 1 reduce performance.

fits_no_version.finding: In a word-triggered backdoored Llama-3.1-8B, a triggered harmful prompt concatenated to a harmful probe strongly shifts the probe's first-token distribution. Benign or untriggered harmful prompts barely shift it (Fig. 3, values only in the figure).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Backdoor triggers distort a harmful probe's refusal distribution, while non-triggered inputs do not.

fits_no_version.finding: Keyword-based trigger ASR of backdoored Llama-3.1-8B falls as poisoned SFT samples drop from 50 to 10 (Fig. 6, figure only). With KL regularization toward the clean model, ASR falls from 60% (λ=0.1) to 15% (λ=100) (Table 14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trigger-conditioned backdoor unalignment strength scales with poison count and is traded off against distributional stealth.

fits_no_version.finding: Detector AUROC peaks at 10 sampled tokens and declines with longer samples. A backdoor trained to start with a refusal prefix and then give harmful content defeats 10-token BEAT (AUROC 47.4) but not 50-token BEAT (96.1) (Fig. 5c, Table 16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal signals in aligned and backdoored models concentrate in the first output tokens, but trained refusal prefixes can hide later harmful content.

record.problems: The safety-behavior examples are qualitative and use selected prompts; they provide no refusal or harmful-compliance rates for the fine-tuned models. The KL plot reports no numerical values in the text. The study’s primary numerical outcomes concern detector performance, not the claim’s safety-behavior measures.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded the BEAT detector AUROC/TPR tables and figures (Sections 5, Appendices E and F) because they measure detection performance rather than harmful compliance or refusal. Excluded the adaptive-attack ASR/defense metrics for the same reason. The study does not report aligned-versus-base KL by response position or compliant-prefill harmful-completion rates.

untested.parts: Unconditional harmful compliance after harmful fine-tuning; backdoor training deliberately keeps refusal on untriggered prompts.
All; its KL is between probe and probe+input on the first token, not aligned vs base by position.
All; the jailbreak section reports detector AUROC on selected successful attacks, not attack success rates.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 labels are dropped: the compliance is induced by design, conditional on a trigger, and shown only in selected qualitative examples. The paper cites Qi et al. 2025 (shallow alignment) only as future work and assumes early-token refusal as a premise.

versions.untested_parts: Tests trigger-conditioned harmful behavior in backdoor-fine-tuned models, but does not establish that a few to a few hundred harmful examples generally remove refusal almost entirely; it reports qualitative examples rather than broad refusal-rate measurements.
No ordinary or benign fine-tuning intervention is tested; benign prompts are concatenated with a probe, not used for fine-tuning.
Does not compare aligned and base models’ per-token KL across response positions. Its KL analysis compares first-output-token distributions for a probe and probe-plus-input.
Does not measure harmful completion rates caused by compliant prefill, suffixes, or decoding changes. The jailbreak experiments report BEAT detection performance.
No localized weights, ranks, or parameter subsets are tested.
Does not test whether training data or objective causes safety shallowness.
Does not test training intended to deepen safety across response positions or its robustness.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Shown word-triggered backdoor examples for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and GPT-3.5-turbo
reader_labels.reason: Each triggered example changes the shown harmful-probe response from refusal to harmful compliance (r1–r6). These are qualitative examples, not broad refusal-rate estimates.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The evidence is limited to particular triggered prompts and examples; it does not show that refusal is removed almost entirely or establish the number of harmful training examples needed (r2, r4, r6).
